match.reason: The closest bank point is about classifying the costs of change and naming staff inertia, not about low-risk strategies such as communication, empowerment, support and incentives that help staff accept change, so it teaches a different idea.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, wording: Incentives are defined in the same bullet as Support, so a student could read incentives as part of support. In the Study Design they are separate low-risk strategies. Give incentives their own bullet.

rejected.title: Overcoming resistance with low-risk strategies
card: Staff may resist change because they fear losing their job, doubt the reason for it, or dislike new routines. Low-risk strategies try to win staff over and keep their trust.
Communication
explaining what is changing, why, and when, and listening to staff concerns in return.
Empowerment
giving staff a say in the change, such as joining a planning team or helping choose how to do the new task.
Support
giving staff training, time and help to learn new ways. Incentives are rewards, such as a bonus or recognition, for taking part in the change.
rejected.remember: Low-risk strategies work with staff: explain, involve, help and reward.

a.q: A manager sets up a team of staff from each section to help plan a new ordering system. Which strategy is this?
opts: Empowerment, as staff have a say in the change
Communication, as staff are told about the change
Support, as staff are given training for the change
Incentives, as staff are paid more for the change
a.why: Staff are helping to plan the change, so they have a say in it. That is empowerment. Communication would only be telling staff or listening to them, and nothing here says they are paid or trained.
a.clue: Look at what the staff are being asked to do.

b.q: Priya owns a bakery chain in Geelong and is bringing in new ovens. Staff worry they will not cope. She runs hands-on lessons on the ovens and gives staff extra practice time. Which strategy is this?
opts: Support, as it helps staff learn to use the new ovens
Incentives, as staff are rewarded for using the ovens
Communication, as staff are told why the ovens changed
Empowerment, as staff get a say in choosing the ovens
b.why: Lessons and practice time help staff learn new ways, which answers their worry about coping. That is support. Empowerment is tempting because staff gain skills, but empowerment means giving staff a say in the change, and here Priya made the choices.
b.clue: Match the strategy to the staff worry.

b.q: Priya owns a bakery chain in Geelong and is bringing in new ovens. Staff worry they will not cope. She runs paid training sessions on the ovens. Which strategy is this mainly?
opts: Support, as it helps staff learn the new ovens
Incentives, as the sessions are paid for staff
Communication, as staff hear about the new ovens
Empowerment, as staff learn to run the new ovens
b.why: Staff fear they will not cope, and training helps them learn the new skill. That is support. Pay for attending is tempting, but it is not a reward for accepting the change, and the training is aimed at the worry.
b.clue: Match the strategy to the staff worry.

a.best: Empowerment, as staff have a say in the change

b.best: Support, as it helps staff learn the new ovens

problems.detail: "Paid training sessions" is ambiguous: it could mean Priya pays for the training or that staff are paid to attend. Under the card's definition (rewards for taking part in the change), being paid to attend could be read as an incentive. "Mainly" keeps support as the best answer, but the stem invites doubt.

The why says pay is "not a reward for accepting the change", but the card defines incentives as rewards for "taking part in" the change. Attending training is taking part, so the why slightly conflicts with the card's wording.

check.summary: The card and question a are sound. In question b, "paid training" is ambiguous and the why's reasoning on incentives does not quite match the card's definition ("taking part" versus "accepting"). Consider rewording the stem, for example "runs training sessions on the ovens during work hours".
